items.explanation: The author argues examinations measure a narrow performance yet decide lives, that the system then organises itself around the test, and that coaching makes the test measure coaching rather than ability. Abolition is explicitly rejected.
options: Examinations measure performance narrowly yet carry life-deciding weight, distorting education itself, so their verdict should be treated as a verdict on a performance rather than on a person.

Coaching improves examinations by making them measure ability more accurately.
items.passage: Every year, millions of students sit examinations that will decide where they study, what they earn and how they are regarded for the rest of their lives. The examination presents itself as a neutral instrument, a fair measure of ability that sorts the deserving from the undeserving. The claim is worth examining, because an examination measures something narrower than it pretends to. It measures performance on a particular day, on a particular set of questions, under particular conditions of stress and preparation. A student who falls ill, who cannot afford coaching, or who thinks slowly but deeply will score lower than the examination claims their ability warrants, and the gap between the score and the ability is not a rounding error but the whole story for the student concerned. Defenders reply that no system is perfect, and that examinations, for all their faults, are fairer than the alternatives: interviews that reward confidence, recommendations that reward connections, portfolios that reward wealth. The reply is fair as far as it goes, but it answers the wrong question. The question is not whether examinations are better than interviews but whether a single high-stakes test should carry the weight it does, when its measurement is so narrow and its consequences so large. A test that decides a life in three hours invites the whole education system to organise itself around it. Teachers teach to the test, students learn to the test, and the curriculum narrows to what can be examined quickly. The subjects that cannot be reduced to a timed question, judgement, originality, moral reasoning, disappear from the classroom, not because they are unimportant but because they are untestable. The result is a system that is efficient at sorting and poor at educating, and the irony is that the sorting itself becomes less accurate as the system adapts to it: when everyone is coached to the test, the test stops measuring ability and starts measuring coaching. None of this means examinations should be abolished. A society needs some way to compare students from different schools, and a well-designed examination is better than patronage. The pressure does not fall evenly. A student from a wealthy family can afford coaching, quiet study space and repeated attempts; a student from a poor family cannot, and the examination, which claims to measure ability, ends up measuring resources. The gap is not a flaw in the design of any particular test but a consequence of treating a single performance as a verdict. When the stakes are high enough, those with resources will always find ways to buy an advantage, and the test will measure the advantage rather than the ability it was designed to capture. The fairest examination in the world cannot fix an unfair starting line. But the weight given to a single examination, and the narrowness of what it measures, should make us cautious about treating its verdict as a verdict on a person rather than on a performance.

items.passage: The idea is seductive in its simplicity. If the planet is warming because greenhouse gases trap heat, why not reflect a little of the sun's energy back into space? Spraying fine particles into the stratosphere, or brightening the clouds above the oceans, could cool the Earth within months, at a cost far lower than rebuilding the world's energy system. The proposal, known as solar radiation management, has moved from science fiction to serious policy discussion, and its advocates make a powerful case. The climate is changing faster than societies are cutting emissions, and a temporary cooling could buy time, preventing the crossing of thresholds that cannot be uncrossed. The case against it is not that it would fail to cool the planet. It is that cooling the planet is not the same as fixing the climate. Reflecting sunlight does nothing about the carbon dioxide accumulating in the oceans, which is acidifying them and threatening the marine food chains on which a billion people depend. It would also have to be maintained indefinitely: stop the spraying and the suppressed warming returns within years, faster than societies could adapt. Worse, the power to set the planet's temperature would fall to whoever controlled the spraying. A country that cooled the Earth to suit its own harvests might dry the monsoon on which another country depends, and there is no institution on Earth capable of governing such a decision fairly. The deepest objection is moral hazard. A cheap technical fix, even a hypothetical one, gives governments an excuse to postpone the hard work of cutting emissions, and the postponement is itself a decision with consequences. There is also the question of who decides when to stop. A programme that cools the planet would create its own constituency: farmers whose harvests depend on the cooler climate, cities whose heatwaves have eased, governments that have built their plans around the new temperature. Each year of spraying would make stopping harder, and the decision to stop would itself become a political crisis. The programme would also interact with the climate in ways that are hard to predict. Cooling the planet unevenly could shift rainfall patterns, drying some regions while flooding others, and the models that predict these effects disagree about where the rain would fall. A decision taken to help one region could harm another, and the harmed region would have no court to appeal to. These uncertainties do not prove the idea should never be tried, but they show that the decision cannot be treated as a purely technical one, to be settled by comparing temperatures. It is a decision about who bears the risk, and no model can answer that question on its own. The honest conclusion is not that solar radiation management should never be researched. It is that the question cannot be answered by engineers alone, because it is a question about who governs the sky, and no one has yet proposed an answer to that.

items.passage: A statue that was taken from a temple two hundred years ago now stands in a museum thousands of miles away, admired by visitors who know nothing of the place it came from. The museum argues that it is a custodian, not an owner: it preserves the statue, studies it, and shows it to the world, and returning it would put it at risk. The country of origin argues that custody without consent is another name for theft, and that a statue kept from the community that made it has lost half its meaning. Both sides have a point, which is what makes the argument difficult. Preservation matters, and some objects returned to unstable places have indeed been damaged or lost. But preservation is not a neutral act. To preserve an object in a foreign museum is also to decide whose story it tells, and the story told in the museum is rarely the story the makers would have told. The honest question is not whether the statue is safer in London or in Lagos but who gets to decide, and on what grounds. The argument is complicated by the fact that many objects were not simply stolen but bought, gifted or exchanged under circumstances that are hard to judge from a distance. A statue sold by a local ruler two centuries ago was a transaction, but it was a transaction between parties of vastly unequal power, and the price paid reflected that inequality. The line between a sale and a seizure is not always sharp, and museums have used that ambiguity to resist claims they find inconvenient. The honest approach is to examine each case on its own facts rather than applying a single rule to all of them. Some objects were clearly looted; some were clearly bought fairly; most lie somewhere between, and the negotiation should reflect that complexity rather than pretending it does not exist. A museum that refuses even to discuss return is not preserving heritage; it is asserting ownership, and ownership asserted over a stolen object is a continuation of the taking, not its end.

items.passage: Do people who speak different languages think differently? The question has divided scholars for a century. The strong version of the claim, that language determines thought, has few defenders left. No one seriously argues that a person cannot think a thought for which their language has no word. The weaker version, that language influences thought, is harder to dismiss. Speakers of languages that mark the future differently save money at different rates, or so one famous study claimed. Speakers of languages with many words for snow were once said to see snow differently, a claim that turned out to rest on shaky counting. The evidence is messy because the question is messy: language, culture and environment move together, and separating their effects is difficult. What the research does show is narrower and more interesting. Language shapes attention: it makes some distinctions easy to notice and others easy to miss. A language that obliges its speakers to mark the direction of an event will make its speakers unusually good at keeping track of direction. The effect is real but modest, a nudge rather than a prison. The research has also produced surprises in the opposite direction. Speakers of languages that lack a future tense are sometimes said to save less, because the future feels less distinct from the present, but the finding is contested, and the effect, if it exists, is small. Speakers of languages with grammatical gender sometimes associate objects with masculine or feminine qualities, but the effect vanishes when the task does not involve language. These small, fragile effects are typical of the field: language nudges thought in the moment of speaking, but the nudge fades when the task changes. The picture that emerges is not of language as a prison or as a window but as a habit, one that shapes what is easy to notice without determining what can be thought. The sensible conclusion is that language is one influence among many on thought, and that the interesting question is not whether it influences thought but when, and how much.

items.explanation: Equal roots require the discriminant to be zero: 36 - 4k = 0, so k = 9. Equivalently the equation is (x - 3)^2 = 0 when k = 9. The discriminant test is the standard condition for repeated roots.
items.question: The equation x^2 - 6x + k = 0 has equal roots. What is k?

items.explanation: The amount is 5000 into 1.10^2 = 5000 into 1.21 = Rs 6,050. The interest is Rs 1,050, which is more than two years of simple interest (Rs 1,000) because the first year's interest earns interest too.
items.question: A sum of Rs 5,000 is invested at 10% compound interest per annum. What is the amount after 2 years, in rupees?

items.explanation: Squaring the unknown sum gives (x + 1/x)^2 = x^2 + 2 + 1/x^2 = 7 + 2 = 9, so x + 1/x = 3, taking the positive root. Working backwards from the square is the key move.
items.question: If x^2 + 1/x^2 = 7, what is x + 1/x? (Take the positive value.)

items.explanation: By Pythagoras the hypotenuse is sqrt(7^2 + 24^2) = sqrt(49 + 576) = sqrt(625) = 25 cm. This is the 7-24-25 Pythagorean triple, the second most common in CAT after 3-4-5.
items.question: In a triangle, two sides are 7 cm and 24 cm and the included angle is 90 degrees. What is the length of the third side, in cm?

items.explanation: The filling rate is 1/6 and the net rate is 1/8, so the leak rate is 1/6 - 1/8 = 1/24 of the tank per hour. The leak alone would empty the full tank in 24 hours. The leak is a negative rate, exactly like an outlet pipe.
items.question: A pipe can fill a tank in 6 hours. Due to a leak, it takes 8 hours to fill the tank. How long would the leak take to empty the full tank, in hours?

items.explanation: The sum of the first n natural numbers is n(n + 1)/2, so for n = 20 it is 20 into 21/2 = 210. Pairing the first and last terms (1 + 20, 2 + 19 and so on) gives ten pairs of 21.
items.question: What is the sum of the first 20 natural numbers?

items.explanation: Numbers leaving remainder 2 on division by 5 are 2, 7, 12, 17, 22 and so on. Checking each mod 7: 17 leaves remainder 3, and it is the first one that does. This is a small Chinese remainder problem, solvable by listing.
items.question: What is the smallest number that leaves remainder 2 when divided by 5 and remainder 3 when divided by 7?

items.explanation: A's capital-months are 20000 into 6 + 15000 into 6 = 210,000, and B's are 30000 into 6 + 35000 into 6 = 390,000. The ratio is 21:39 = 7:13, so A gets 7/20 of Rs 26,000 = Rs 9,100. Profit shares follow capital multiplied by time, not just capital.
items.question: A and B invest Rs 20,000 and Rs 30,000 in a business. After 6 months, A withdraws Rs 5,000 and B adds Rs 5,000. At the end of the year the profit is Rs 26,000. What is A's share, in rupees?

items.explanation: The perimeter is 2 into (length + breadth) = 2 into 20 = 40 cm. This is the one routine mensuration question in the mock.
items.question: What is the perimeter of a rectangle with length 12 cm and breadth 8 cm, in cm?

items.explanation: The total age is 5 into 30 = 150 years. Removing the 10-year-old leaves 140 years across 4 members, an average of 35 years. The average rises because the removed member was well below average.
items.question: The average age of 5 members of a family is 30 years. The youngest member is 10 years old. What is the average age of the remaining 4 members, in years?

items.explanation: Since 16 = 2^4, we have x - 1 = 4, so x = 5. Writing both sides as powers of the same base is the standard move for exponential equations.
items.question: If 2^(x-1) = 16, what is x?

items.explanation: The favourable pairs are 6 into 4 = 24 (one red and one blue), and the total pairs are C(10, 2) = 45, so the probability is 24/45 = 8/15. Alternatively, red-then-blue gives (6/10) into (4/9) = 4/15 and blue-then-red the same, totalling 8/15.
items.question: A bag has 6 red and 4 blue balls. Two balls are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that one is red and one is blue?

items.explanation: His savings are 40% of his income, so 0.40 into income = 8000, giving income = Rs 20,000. The savings percentage is the complement of the spending percentage.
items.question: A man spends 60% of his income and saves Rs 8,000 per month. What is his monthly income, in rupees?

items.explanation: Since 48 = 2^4 into 3, the sum of its factors is (2^5 - 1)/(2 - 1) into (3^2 - 1)/(3 - 1) = 31 into 4 = 124. Listing the factors (1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 48) and adding confirms 124.
items.question: What is the sum of all factors of 48?

items.explanation: Let the smaller be n. Then n(n + 2) = 143, so n^2 + 2n - 143 = 0, factoring as (n + 13)(n - 11) = 0. The positive root is n = 11, and the pair is 11 and 13. Checking 11 into 13 = 143 confirms it.
items.question: The product of two consecutive odd numbers is 143. What is the smaller number?

items.explanation: LEVEL has 5 letters with L repeated twice and E repeated twice, so the count is 5!/(2! into 2!) = 120/4 = 30. Repeated letters divide the factorial count, or the arrangements would be overcounted.
items.question: How many different words can be formed using all the letters of the word LEVEL?

items.explanation: From 2 pi r = 44 we get r = 44 into 7/(2 into 22) = 7 cm. The area is pi r^2 = (22/7) into 49 = 154 sq cm. The circumference determines the radius, and the radius determines the area.
items.question: A circle has circumference 44 cm. What is its area, in sq cm? (Take pi = 22/7)

items.explanation: Speed is distance divided by time, 150/2.5 = 60 km/h. The decimal divisor is the only wrinkle; 1500/25 = 60.
items.question: If a car covers 150 km in 2.5 hours, what is its speed, in km/h?

items.explanation: The sum of the roots of x^2 + px + c = 0 is -p. Here -p = -5, so p = 5. The sign is the trap: the coefficient p is the negative of the root sum.
items.question: If the sum of the roots of x^2 + px + 6 = 0 is -5, what is p?

items.explanation: The product is odd only when both dice show odd numbers, which happens with probability (3/6) into (3/6) = 1/4. So the product is even with probability 1 - 1/4 = 3/4. The complement is easier to count than the direct cases.
items.question: Two dice are thrown. What is the probability that the product of the two numbers is even?
